Is SpaceX Just a Mess?
 
Plus, a disguised pitch for private credit and the superrich are tearing down mega mansions
 
 
ORIN LOUIS/ZUMA PRESS
 

As France tries to restore order to the public finances and the streets, the government faces a significant financial challenge: an unusual reliance on foreign investors who no longer have a strong reason to come to its rescue.

 

More than most other major economies, the French government depends on overseas lenders, especially in Japan, to fund its deficit. Almost 55% of French debt was owned outside the country last year, according to the European Union’s data service. In the U.S., the figure stood at 31% and in Japan, 13%.

 

For years, foreigners loved France’s debt market, one of the world’s biggest. The bonds were easy to trade and yielded a bit more than other economies, but were perceived as safe, backed up by the European Union’s second-largest economy. Whenever yields rose, foreigners would swoop in to take advantage of the higher returns on offer.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

IBM will need to strike some deals in order to hit its target for 5% constant-currency revenue growth next year, Morgan Stanley analysts write in a note. Even assuming a better-than-expected infrastructure cycle and an acceleration in organic software growth next year, the company is not on track to hit the target, the analysts write. “This means we are on IBM M&A watch for the remainder of the year, as it’s the final bridge towards IBM reaching Street revenue forecasts in 2027, in our view,” they write. They maintain an equal-weight rating and bump up their price target by $2 to $240. Shares of IBM fall 1.3% to $248.27. (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

 

Although much of the focus among prediction markets is coming from attracting more institutional money to the space, retail investors have been wielding more power in directing markets than many realize, says JB Mackenzie of Robinhood. Speaking at the NEXTPreidict summit in New York, Mackenzie uses the example of airline stocks during the Covid-19 epidemic as retail investors flexing their control. With the advent of widespread proliferation of smart phones, these investors are not much behind in computing capabilities to other more-established technologies trading, Mackenzie says. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com)
